newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Protests damages Milosevic's bid to repair image.
newsitem.headline: Protests damages Milosevic's bid to repair image.

text.p: Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic has suffered severe damage at home and abroad from a tide of street demonstrations but the former communist party chief is betting the protests will run out of steam.

Milosevic looked well on the way to burying his political opponents and rehabilitating himself with Western powers until his blatant move to cancel opposition victories in local elections this month, analysts said on Thursday.

The annulment of poll results sparked public outage and led to street protests in Belgrade and across the country, breathing life into ailing opposition parties and tapping deep discontent over plummeting living standards.
"It was a miscalculation," Zoran Djindjic, a leader of the Zajedno (Together) coalition, told Reuters.
"He had the chance to minimise the importance of the local elections...to prevent us from exerting real authority at the municipal level and to let the defeat pass quietly.
"Instead, he turned the local elections into presidential elections."
Opposition leaders were ecstatic about the scale of their poll victory and subsequent protests, especially in former Milosevic strongholds in industrial towns.
But they were hesitant about how to proceed, aware they had raised hopes of fundamental change for the first time since similar protests were crushed in 1991.
"I hope we're going to be able to control these emotions," Djindjic said.
Opposition activists, who have tried to turn the protests into a referendum on Milosevic's nine-year rule, acknowledged the demonstrations could not continue indefinitely.
Zajedno leaders said they would order strikes and widespread civil disobedience to turn up the heat on Milosevic, whose police have exercised restraint despite some stone throwing.
But the opposition had yet to show it could mobilise workers in sufficient numbers to shut down cities.
"I think Milosevic will try to ignore this, in the belief the protest could exhaust itself," said a Western diplomat.

The crowds on Serbia's streets also obscured the fact that Milosevic still had a loyal minority -- mainly pensioners -- supporting him in a country lacking democratic traditions and accustomed to authoritarian leaders.
Milosevic's efforts to woo the West and gain international acceptance were undercut badly by the poll fiasco only days before a London conference on the Bosnia peace process.
The opposition has succeeded in drawing international attention to its cause but Western diplomats remained sceptical that all the coalition members had forsaken Serb nationalist goals.
Milosevic, who signed the Dayton peace treaty a year ago, was still considered by Western countries as a guarantor helping keep the peace in Bosnia.
Although Milosevic may not be on the verge of being toppled, political analysts said his reputation for invincibility had been dealt a blow.
Milosevic could still rely on "tools of repression" -- police and state television -- to remain in power indefinitely, said Novak Kilibarda, an opposition leader and longtime critic of Milosevic.
"I'm convinced that this is the beginning of the end of the dictatorship. But I'm not sure long it will take... Unfortunatley a dictatorship can hang on a long time," Kilibarda said.
